title: When Should You Seal a New Asphalt Driveway? After 6-12 Months
metaDescription: Seal a new asphalt driveway after 6 to 12 months, once it has cured through one full warm season. Readiness checks, timing by climate and first-coat tips.
h1: When Should You Seal a New Asphalt Driveway?
keyword: when should you seal a new asphalt driveway
keywords: when to seal new asphalt driveway
how long should you wait to seal new asphalt
when to sealcoat a new asphalt driveway
how soon to seal new asphalt driveway
how long to wait to seal a new driveway
should you seal a new driveway
intro:
You should seal a new asphalt driveway after about 6 to 12 months, and only once it has cured through at least one full warm season. Heat is what drives the light oils out of fresh binder, so a driveway paved in May is usually ready far sooner than one paved in October.

Sealing earlier does not protect anything. Fresh blacktop is already dark, tight and water-shedding, and a coat applied in the first few months holds in oils that still need to escape. This guide explains how long to wait, three checks that tell you the pavement is ready, how climate and paving date shift the timing, and how to care for the surface until then.
quickAnswer: Wait roughly 6 to 12 months, or one full summer, before the first coat of sealer goes on new asphalt. Hot, sunny regions sit at the short end; cold climates and fall paving jobs often wait until the second summer. Seal once the gloss has faded to charcoal, the surface resists a thumbnail on a warm day and water soaks in instead of beading.

sections.heading: When Should You Seal a New Asphalt Driveway? The Short Answer
sections.body:
Plan the first seal for 6 to 12 months after paving, and count warm months rather than calendar months. A new driveway needs at least one full season of hot weather before it is ready for a coating, because that heat is what pushes the lighter oils out of the binder and lets the surface firm up.

| When it was paved | Curing before winter | Typical first seal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spring | A full summer | Late summer that year to the next spring |
| Early summer | Most of a summer | The following spring or early summer |
| Late summer | A few warm weeks | The following summer |
| Fall | Almost none | The summer after a full warm season |
| Hot, sunny climate | Fast curing | Short end of 6-12 months; some contractors use about 90 days as a floor |
| Cold climate | Paused for months | Often a full year, or the second summer |

Treat the table as a starting point. The readiness checks further down tell you more about your own driveway than the month on the calendar does. When in doubt, wait. A sound new driveway loses nothing by going an extra season unsealed, while a coat that goes on too soon can leave you with a soft, blotchy surface.

If your paving contractor left written care instructions, follow them first. They know the mix they laid, and some sealer labels also state a minimum age for new asphalt.

sections.heading: Why Can't You Seal New Asphalt Right Away?
sections.body:
Because the pavement is still curing. Hot-mix asphalt is crushed stone and sand held together by asphalt binder, a heavy petroleum product. When it is laid, that binder still contains lighter oils that leave slowly over the following months. That is why a new driveway smells faintly of tar on hot afternoons, looks almost wet and takes a dent from a kickstand.

### What does a coat of sealer do to fresh binder?

Two things. First, the sealer forms a film across the top that slows the escape of those light oils, so the surface can stay soft longer and collect more scuffs and dents. Second, an oily surface is a poor base for a water-based coating. Early coats are more likely to wear unevenly, discolor or come away in patches.

### Is there any protection to gain?

Not yet. Sealer exists to replace what the sun takes away from the top of the binder through oxidation. A brand-new driveway has not lost any of that. Its surface is still rich, black and water-repellent on its own, so an early coat is money spent on protection the pavement does not need.

### What do pavers and sealer makers say?

Many paving contractors put the waiting period in their care sheets, and many sealer labels tell you not to apply the product to new asphalt within a set window. When the two sources agree with the readiness checks below, you can seal with confidence.

sections.heading: How Long Should You Wait to Seal New Asphalt?
sections.body:
Six to twelve months is the common guidance for residential driveways. Some contractors in very hot regions use about 90 days as a bare minimum, and many in cold regions ask for a full year. The real requirement is one complete warm season, because cold months add very little curing.

### The rule of thumb

Let the driveway cure through one full summer, then seal it during the next stretch of warm, dry weather. A driveway paved in May gets the whole summer to cure and is often ready by the following spring. A driveway paved in October gets almost no curing weather before winter, so its first coat usually waits until the summer after next.

### Is waiting longer than a year a problem?

Rarely. A well-built driveway will not break down in any meaningful way during a second unsealed year. Waiting too long only becomes an issue when the surface has clearly turned gray and water soaks straight in, which is a sign that oxidation has started and the first coat is now overdue.

### Does crack repair have to wait too?

No. The waiting period is for the coating, not for repairs. A new driveway should not crack in its first year, so if one appears along a seam or edge, call the installer first because their workmanship warranty may cover it. If it does not, clean and fill the crack right away so water cannot reach the base.

sections.heading: How Do You Know New Asphalt Is Ready to Seal?
sections.body:
Check three things: color, firmness and how the surface handles water. Each check takes about a minute, and when all three agree, the driveway is ready for its first coat.

### Has the color faded from black gloss to charcoal?

Fresh asphalt is deep black with a slight sheen. As the surface oils leave and the top begins to oxidize, it turns a flatter charcoal and the small stones in the mix become easier to see. The change starts where the sun hits hardest, so compare a sunny section with a shaded one near the house. When neither looks glossy, the surface has firmed up.

### Does the surface resist a thumbnail on a warm day?

Test on a warm afternoon, in a spot that gets little traffic. Press a thumbnail or the edge of a coin hard into the pavement. Fresh asphalt takes a clear mark; cured asphalt pushes back. Also look for new dents from parked tires, chair legs or bike stands. If new marks keep appearing on hot days, the binder is still soft.

### Does water soak in instead of beading?

Sprinkle water over a few areas. On young asphalt, water beads and runs off. As the surface oxidizes and opens up, water starts to darken the pavement and sink in. That absorption is the point where the asphalt has given up some of its natural protection, and where a sealer starts earning its cost.

### What if the checks disagree?

Keep waiting. A driveway that still looks glossy and dents easily is not ready, even if water has started to soak in at one sunny edge. Once all three signs line up, pick your day using our guide to [what temperature to seal a driveway](/what-temperature-to-seal-driveway/), which lists the minimums most labels set.

sections.heading: How Do Climate and Paving Date Change the Timing?
sections.body:
Hot, sunny places shorten the wait and cold places stretch it, because asphalt cures in earnest only when it is warm. The month it was paved decides how much heat it gets before the first winter.

### Hot, sunny regions

In the desert Southwest, Texas and much of the Southeast, long stretches of high pavement temperature push oils out quickly, and strong UV starts oxidizing the surface early. A spring paving job in these areas is often ready by fall or the following spring, at the short end of the range.

### Cold regions

In the upper Midwest, the Northeast and mountain areas, curing nearly stops for several months each year. Count only warm-season time. A driveway laid in late summer or fall in Minnesota or Maine may get just a few useful weeks before winter, which often pushes the first seal to the second summer.

### Mild, damp regions

The Pacific Northwest sits between the two. Temperatures are moderate but summers are dependably dry, so a driveway paved in spring or early summer usually cures through that first summer. The catch is the short sealing window before fall rain arrives. If you miss it, aim for mid-summer of the next year.

### Shade on part of the driveway

Even one driveway can cure at two speeds. The strip under a tree or along the north side of the house stays cooler and cures more slowly than the sunny stretch by the street. Always run your readiness checks in the shadiest section. If that area still dents easily, give the whole driveway more time rather than sealing half of it.

sections.heading: How Do You Care for a New Asphalt Driveway in the First Year?
sections.body:
Keep traffic off for the first few days, then spend the first year protecting the soft surface from scuffs, point loads, edge damage and spills. None of this involves sealer.

### When can you drive on it?

Keep vehicles off for as long as your paver specifies, often about three days, and longer in a heat wave. After that, drive normally but avoid turning the steering wheel while the car is not moving. Those power-steering scuffs are the most common cosmetic damage on new blacktop, especially on hot afternoons. Shift where you park now and then so the same tire spots are not loaded all summer.

### Which point loads should you avoid?

Anything with a small, heavy footprint can sink into warm binder: motorcycle and bike kickstands, car jacks, trailer tongue jacks, ladder feet and heavy planters. Put a scrap of plywood under them. If you can, keep moving trucks, dumpsters and RVs off the driveway for the first year.

### How do you protect the edges and handle spills?

The edges are the weakest part of new asphalt because nothing supports them on the outside. Keep tires off them and build soil and turf up against them for support. Gasoline, oil and other petroleum spills soften fresh binder, so blot them quickly and rinse the spot. If a drip does set in, our guide on [how to remove oil stains from a driveway](/how-to-remove-oil-stains-from-driveway/) covers the water-based methods that are safe on blacktop.

### What cleaning does it need?

Very little: sweep or blow off debris, rinse it now and then with a hose and pull edge weeds as soon as they appear. If moss starts in a shady corner, deal with it early using the steps in our guide on [how to remove moss from an asphalt driveway](/how-to-remove-moss-from-asphalt-driveway/). A driveway that gets a careful first year reaches its first seal in better shape, and that first coat goes on more easily.

sections.heading: How Do You Apply the First Seal on a New Driveway?
sections.body:
Clean the surface, let it dry fully, and apply thin coats of a water-based sealer at the label rate on a dry, mild day. On a properly cured driveway this is usually the easiest seal job the pavement will ever get.

### How much prep is needed?

Not much. A first-time driveway should have few cracks, little oxidation and only light dirt. Sweep it, wash it, treat any oil drips with an oil spot primer, and let it dry completely before you open a pail.

### One coat or two?

Either works. Because the surface is still fairly tight, the first coat often spreads farther than it would on an old driveway, so you may land near the high end of the label's coverage range. Many owners put down two thin coats to build an even film; others use one coat on a driveway in excellent condition. Do not lay it on thick, which leads to tracking and peeling.

### Which sealer type suits a new driveway?

A quality water-based asphalt emulsion or acrylic-modified sealer is the usual choice, and it is legal everywhere. Coal-tar sealers are restricted or banned in several states and many towns because of concerns about the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons they contain. Our ranked [asphalt driveway sealer reviews](/best-asphalt-driveway-sealer-reviews/) and broader [driveway sealer picks](/best-driveway-sealer/) sort the main options.

### What weather does it need?

Most labels call for air and surface temperatures of at least 50°F and rising, no rain for 24 hours or more, and nights warm enough for the coating to keep curing. Plan for a run of dry, mild days in late spring, summer or early fall, depending on your region.

sections.heading: Should New Asphalt Be Sealed at All?
sections.body:
Not at first, but in most climates yes over the long run. Once the pavement starts to oxidize, a sealer slows that aging and keeps water out of the surface. Driveways that are never sealed tend to fade to gray, turn brittle and crack sooner.

### What does sealing actually do?

A sealer coat replaces the binder the sun strips from the top layer, fills fine surface voids, resists oil and gas drips and gives the driveway a uniform dark color. It does not add structural strength, and it will not fix a weak base or deep cracks.

### Are there reasons some owners skip it?

Yes. Some owners accept a gray surface in exchange for lower upkeep, and a well-built driveway on a good base can last a long time with crack filling alone. The trade-offs are covered in our guide to [sealing asphalt driveway pros and cons](/sealing-asphalt-driveway-pros-and-cons/). For most homeowners, a coat every few years is one of the cheapest ways to stretch the life of the pavement.

### What does it cost?

The first seal on a new driveway is usually the cheapest you will ever do, because there are few cracks to fill and little prep. Our guide on [how much it costs to seal a driveway](/how-much-does-it-cost-to-seal-a-driveway/) breaks down DIY and contractor costs.

sections.heading: How Often Should You Seal After the First Coat?
sections.body:
Roughly every two to three years for most residential driveways. Sun, traffic and climate all move that interval, so let a quick water test each spring tell you when the current coat has worn through.

| Driveway age | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Day 0 to about 3 days | Keep all traffic off |
| First year | Drive gently, protect edges, keep point loads off, clean spills |
| About 6-12 months, or after one summer | First seal, once readiness checks pass |
| Every spring | Inspect and fill cracks wider than about 1/8 inch |
| Roughly every 2-3 years | Reseal once water soaks in again |
| Around 15-20 years and up | Assess for overlay or replacement |

### Where does crack repair fit?

Crack filling is the other half of upkeep. Check the surface each spring once freeze-thaw season ends and fill cracks promptly so water cannot reach the base. With that routine, a residential asphalt driveway can often last 15 to 20 years or more, depending on the base and the climate.

### Can you seal too often?

Yes. Annual coats pile up into a thick film that can crack and flake on its own, separate from the pavement below. A two-to-three-year rhythm keeps protection in place without that buildup and keeps costs reasonable.

mistakes.title: Sealing Within Months of Paving
mistakes.body: A coat that goes on too early traps light oils that still need to escape and sits on a slick surface it cannot grip. The usual results are a surface that stays soft, uneven color and sealer that peels. Wait for one full warm season and for the color, firmness and water checks to agree.

mistakes.title: Counting Winter as Curing Time
mistakes.body: Asphalt cures in heat. A driveway paved in October has barely changed by April, even though six months have passed. Count only warm-season time, and in cold regions expect a fall paving job to get its first coat in the second summer.

mistakes.title: Treating Normal Softness as a Defect
mistakes.body: Tire scuffs and small dents on a hot day are normal for new asphalt, and most fade as the surface firms up. Sealer will not remove them, and an early coat can slow the curing that would. Use plywood under point loads and vary your parking spot instead.

mistakes.title: Letting Heavy Loads On in Year One
mistakes.body: Moving trucks, dumpsters, RVs and trailer jacks can press lasting dips into fresh asphalt, worst of all near the unsupported edges. If heavy equipment must come in, lay plywood to spread the weight, keep it off the edges and schedule it for a cool morning.

mistakes.title: Forgetting the Driveway Once It Is Ready
mistakes.body: The opposite mistake is letting years slip by after the surface is ready. When water soaks in and the color turns gray, oxidation is underway. Getting the first coat on within a year or so of readiness keeps the pavement in good shape and makes every later seal easier.

faqs.q: How long should you wait to seal new asphalt?
faqs.a: Wait about six to twelve months, and judge it by warm weather rather than the calendar. The driveway should cure through at least one full summer first. Hot climates are often ready at the short end, while a fall paving job in a cold climate may need to wait for the second summer. Seal once the gloss is gone, the surface resists a thumbnail and water soaks in.

faqs.q: What happens if you seal new asphalt too soon?
faqs.a: An early coat can trap light oils in the binder, so the surface stays soft longer and scuffs or dents more easily. Sealer also bonds poorly to an oily surface, which can show up as blotchy color, uneven wear or peeling. You gain no protection in return, because fresh asphalt has not oxidized and already sheds water by itself.

Yes, eventually, but not right away. New asphalt needs no sealer for its first 6 to 12 months because its surface is still rich in binder and sheds water on its own. Once it has cured and starts to oxidize, sealing every two to three years slows graying, brittleness and cracking, which is one of the cheapest ways to extend the driveway life.

faqs.q: When to sealcoat a new asphalt driveway in a cold climate?
faqs.a: Usually in the second summer if it was paved in late summer or fall, and the following summer if it was paved in spring. Cold months add almost no curing, so count only warm-season time. Pick a stretch of days with air and surface temperatures at or above 50°F and rising, and no rain forecast for at least 24 hours.

faqs.q: Can I drive on my new asphalt driveway right away?
faqs.a: Not right away. Most paving contractors advise keeping cars off for about three days, and longer in very hot weather. After that you can drive normally, but avoid turning the wheels while the car is stopped and vary where you park through the first summer. Follow your installer instructions if they differ, since they know the mix and conditions.

faqs.q: Is it okay to fill cracks in a new driveway before sealing?
faqs.a: Yes. The waiting period applies to the sealer coat, not to crack repair. A new driveway should not crack in its first year, so contact the installer first because it may be covered by their warranty. If not, clean the crack and fill it promptly with an asphalt crack filler so water cannot reach the base layer underneath.

faqs.q: What sealer should I use for the first coat on new asphalt?
faqs.a: A quality water-based asphalt emulsion or acrylic-modified sealer suits most new driveways and is legal everywhere. Coal-tar sealers are restricted or banned in several states and many towns because of health and environmental concerns. Apply thin coats at the coverage rate on the label, and choose a dry stretch of mild weather for the job.

bottomLine: Leave new asphalt unsealed for its first 6 to 12 months and let one full warm season do the curing. Protect the soft surface from scuffs, point loads and spills in the meantime, then seal when the gloss has faded, a thumbnail no longer leaves a mark and water soaks in. Use thin coats of a water-based sealer on a dry, mild day, reseal every two to three years and fill cracks each spring, and a residential driveway can give you 15 to 20 years or more.
